preamble: The voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ] becoming the labio-velar glide [w] involves both voicing and the loss of friction. The classic case is Japanese: by the 11th century, Early Middle Japanese medial /ɸ/ (from earlier *p) had merged with /w/ between vowels. This is why 'river' is written かは (kafa) in historical kana orthography but is pronounced kawa. In Late Middle Japanese the glide remained before /a/, while before other vowels it was lost or became [j] (iɸe > ije 'house'). /o/ itself was then pronounced [wo], as in [towo] 'far'. Non-medial ɸ was not affected and later became [h].

examples.note: Intervocalic ɸ merged with w by the 11th century; the historical spelling かは survived until the 1946 kana reform.
/o/ and /wo/ had merged as [wo]; this later became [o], giving modern tō.

sources: Frellesvig, B. (2010). A History of the Japanese Language. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511778322
